utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [French interpretation on English channel] I'll try it again. Good afternoon to everybody. The next witness should be brought in, please. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, everyone. Just to let you know that some translations have been up-loaded: P16C, P149, P665B, P667B, P851A, P851B, P661B, P845B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. They will be now exhibits, with the given numbers, and we are grateful for the work the Translation Unit has performed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Welcome to the Tribunal. Would you please read aloud the affirmation to tell the truth which is shown -- on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down. First, the Prosecutor, Mr. McCloskey, will have some questions for you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you first state your name, and tell us your profession.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: My full name is Richard Vernon Stafford Wright, and I am an archaeologist.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I will soon be reading a brief summary of your prior testimonies, but I just -- to try to clarify right off, my summary says you are an emeritus professor of anthropology from university. Can you explain how it is that you're an archaeologist, but that your formal description is a professor of anthropology?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. The profession of anthropology in many universities includes archaeology and physical anthropology. In the forensic field, particularly in -- yes, in the forensic field, there is a distinction between anthropology, which should be called physical anthropology, and archaeology. At the University of Sydney, I was in the Department of Anthropology, had the chair of anthropology, but I was an archaeologist.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we'll do a short explanation of that as it fits your testimony a little bit later. Have you had a chance to review your testimony in the Popovic and Krstic cases?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you pointed out a mistake in the Popovic testimony, I believe. Do you remember what that was that you wanted to clear up?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: At one point, I was asked the number of graves I had exhumed in 1998, and I said two primary graves and seven secondary graves. In fact, it was one primary grave, and not two, in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And at this point, I think I will read a brief 92 bis summary to set the scene for us. Professor Richard Wright testified for the OTP before this Tribunal in the trial of Radislav Krstic in May 2000 and in the trial of Vujadin Popovic et al. in February 2007. Professor Wright is an emeritus professor of anthropology at the University of Sydney, in Australia. In 1998, 1999 and 2000, Professor Wright served as chief archaeologist for the detection and exhumation of mass graves associated with the fall of Srebrenica. Professor Wright also worked as chief archaeologist for the OTP in the exhumation of various other mass graves involved in other Prosecution cases, including graves at Brcko and the exhumation in Croatia of a mass grave containing Serb civilians. Professor Wright supervised the exhumation of Srebrenica mass graves, including the removal and accounting of human remains and artefacts from mass graves for their transportation to the morgue for examination by anthropologists and forensic pathologists. Professor Wright testified regarding the exhumations of the primary graves of Petkovci Dam, Kozluk, and Glogova 1, and of the secondary grave-sites at Liplje, Hodzici, Cancari, and Zeleni Jadar. He prepared three reports and one interim report summarising those exhumations. Professor Wright and his team were able to link the primary graves to the secondary graves through examination of transported soil, rocks, artefacts, and other information gained. Professor Wright also conducted some examination of the artefacts found in the graves he exhumed. He observed that the documents found attest to the Muslim affinity of some of the people. He explained how he was able to determine the time-frame the victims at grave-sites were killed based on examination and analysis of Seiko watches worn by the victims. With regard to Kozluk, Professor Wright determined that many of the bodies recovered were blindfolded and/or had ligatures binding their hands behind their backs. He also discovered bullets embedded in the soil underneath the bodies at this site. These factors led him to conclude that Kozluk was a place of execution as well as a mass grave-site. Professor Wright noted that some of the bodies in the Glogova grave he exhumed showed signs of blast damage. In addition, parts of exploded grenades were found with some of the bodies, together with rifle bullets. Professor Wright determined from the information gained from his own inspections and from OTP investigators that some of the objects considered to be from the Kravica warehouse were found in the Glogova grave he exhumed. Professor Wright also supervised the preliminary excavation or probing of an additional 21 secondary grave-sites along the Cancari Road, the Hodzici Road, Liplje, and Zeleni Jadar areas during the 1998 season. He explained the process used to identify the sites and testified that a conservative estimate would suggest an additional 2.571 bodies exist in those unexhumed graves. Now, I have a list of the various exhibits and their numbers that came in through you in the last trial, but I also have one that was a bit separate, and so we need to call up 65 ter 6555. And, Professor Wright, this is a document by you entitled "Interim Report on Excavation and Exhumations at Glogova Site 1, Grave L, Carried Out in September 2000."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I don't want to get into this with you, I just wondered if you can identify this front page and tell us if this is a report that you provided the OTP for use in its trials.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: That is my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And how is it, just briefly, that you ended up doing this interim report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: When we had finished at Glogova, we had established some seven sites for investigating, and I was asked by the investigator, Jean Ruez, to provide him with an interim report on this particular grave. He didn't explain, but I provided this report earlier than the main report for the Glogova site.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right, thank you. And, Mr. President, I have the numbers before me of the exhibits in the chart. They are P869 through 891, as well as this 65 ter 6555, and I would offer all that material into evidence. And that should be a complete version of the 92 bis package -- 94 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I'm not sure if you asked the witness, Professor Wright, if he would provide the same answers in this trial if he would be asked in the same way as in the Popovic trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You're absolutely correct. I left that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Professor Wright, if you were asked the same questions in that trial, would your answers be the same, aside, of course, from the one mistake you've identified?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, they would be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. President. Now I would -- with the proper foundation laid, I would offer the material into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. The documents P869 - it's the transcript of the Popovic case - will be received, and as well the documents P870 to P891, except P881, which has no translation yet; in that case, pending translation. And was the interim report we have on the screen now used in that Popovic trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, it was, Mr. President. It came in through another witness, I think Mr. Janc. It came in through him in one of his summary testimonies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That will be received as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 6555 will be Exhibit P1014.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please carry on, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, Professor Wright, we -- your reports and your testimony speak for themselves, so we'll just -- I just want to briefly touch on a few of the basics to help us put everything into context. Can you give us a brief explanation of the differences between your profession as an archaeologist, the professions that worked with you, of anthropology and forensic pathology. The Court has heard these terms through various times, but you're really the first expert, I believe, that's talked about it. So you, as an archaeologist, can you just briefly describe your job and how these other professions fit in with your work, if they did.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. Archaeologists essentially examine the soil and the contents of the soil, and recover the material. They're experts in the engineering aspects of big holes, safety concerns using machinery. They're experts in recording where information -- where artefacts and bodies come from as they're removed so that we can reconstruct the whole form of a grave. And we know about conservation. The anthropologists -- there were anthropologists with archaeological knowledge on my exhumations, and the reason why they were there is they could excavate, but they could also track a body. They knew what bones come from which parts of the body and so were able to make sense of an often contorted mass of bodies. Back at the morgue, in an area where I had no responsibility, the anthropologists evaluate the age of a person at death, the sex of the person, quite often any trauma that the skeleton has suffered, and then the pathologists sign off, I suppose you could say, sign off on the cause and manner of death. So there are these three components: The work at the grave, which is supervised by archaeologists, and with anthropologists involved; the work at the morgue, where anthropologists work on the remains; and then the pathologists, who look for the cause and manner of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And as we noted in the summary, in your testimony at one site, you gave your opinion on -- that at Kozluk, people had been executed, in your view, based on what you had seen as an archaeologist. Were you in any way taking over or interfering with the pathologist's role in determining cause of death by coming to that conclusion or not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I think I would take it as a fairly safe assumption that when I see people who have been shot, I can recognise bullet holes, I have plenty of experience, and when I see their hands tied behind their backs and they're wearing blindfolds, I would come to the conclusion that they had been executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And is coming to conclusions based on what you view in a dig and what you examine, is that a normal part of archaeology or would someone suggest you were speculating outside of your field?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I would not, in the case of a body that was found in a grave and had no gun-shot wounds and no other signs of trauma, and -- I wouldn't start to speculate about the way in which that person died. But in the case of some of the sites that I worked on in Bosnia, I think it would be obvious to non-experts what has happened; certainly obvious to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is telling the story of what you see part of what an archaeologist does, putting your observations together?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. An archaeologist needs to be careful not to go beyond their expertise and what is obvious, but I knew that these remains were going to go to other experts, and, nevertheless, I felt that I should describe the context in which I saw these bodies. Otherwise, they go to the morgue and there's no background information. Blindfolds may fall off during transport, ligatures behind the back may fall off during transport to the morgue. So I was always conscious of the need to make interim observations in case the material never reached the morgue. That was a possibility, given the insecurity of the area. But I don't consider I went beyond what -- beyond my level of expertise, and many of these observations were, I would say, self-evident.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we won't go into this now, but is it fair to say that there are, well, probably literally thousands, if not more, photographs and video that you documented your work in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. In addition to my reports, there were the logs that we kept which list each body and give some of its properties. There were body sheets that were filled out by the excavator, showing how the body was lying, and any other artefacts associated with the body, and there was a complete photographic record that was officially logged so that each artefact -- with the exception, as time went on, of shell cases, each artefact that would be properly associated with a body was photographed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And His Honours and Her Honour have heard lots of evidence about primary and secondary graves. And you worked, we know from your reports, on the Petkovci grave, which you determined to be a primary disturbed grave. Can you just briefly tell the Court how you, as the chief archaeologist, determined that this was a disturbed grave, just in brief terms?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. Can I just go back one point and just define some of the terms?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: The first term that I use is "an execution site," a place where I interpret people were killed. They are then put into a grave, which we have examples at Kozluk and at Petkovci Dam. They're put into a grave. Later, about three months later, from aerial images we have, these bodies or some of the bodies out of these primary graves were removed and taken up into the hills, essentially, and put into secondary graves. So there's the execution site. The primary grave is normally at the execution site, but not in the case of Glogova. That's removed. The primary graves may remain undisturbed, but in cases I looked at, they didn't remain undisturbed; people had taken bodies out and put them into secondary graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. That's very helpful. Just tell us a little bit about Petkovci.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Petkovci Dam, I was told by the investigators, was a primary grave, the place of execution being at the dam. The place that I saw on aerial images was -- and that I went to, the place was in the structure of the dam. There was a big stone supporting platform to hold the wall of the dam back. And I was told that this was undisturbed, and the aerial images that I saw indicated it was undisturbed. But when we excavated it, we found that there were no bodies in place. I mean, a primary grave, by definition, the bodies are lying there. There was just bits and pieces of bodies as we went down through this two metres or so of rocks, scattered bits of clothing, limb bones lying on a ramp that had been used to get into that grave and remove the bodies, cut marks of the machine that had scooped the bodies out. So it was clear to me that this was certainly not a primary grave. It had been, archaeologists use the term "robbed" in a non-pejorative sense, the don't imply thieving, but it had been disturbed, more general terminology and it was not a primary grave, and I reported this back to ICTY. And I understand, though I haven't seen it, that there was an image which had been missed, that it showed that the site was disturbed in October, I think, or late September.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you mean it wasn't a primary, undisturbed grave or not a primary grave?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: It's a primary grave, but it had been disturbed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. And did you also have a chance to exhume what you believed to be secondary graves?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, most of my work has been done on secondary graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Since you just talked about the dam and its sort of unique structure, did you see -- did you work on any exhumations of secondary graves that you felt were related to the dam primary grave?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, I did. The site of Liplje -- I can't remember the number. May I consult my notes to answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Can you tell us what you've --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I have a copy of my report on the 1998 exhumations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: The site -- you asked me did I see a site which I would attribute to the Petkovci Dam, and the site is Liplje number 2, is the number we gave to it. And the reason why I thought the bodies had come from this dam was that it was unique amongst any other secondary grave I'd looked at, where there were large lumps of rock, cut limestone rock, which were foreign to the area. The bodies were -- there were hardly any complete bodies. They were smashed up, and I concluded that they had come from the Petkovci Dam or some similar -- such similar structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This cut limestone rock that you saw, when you say "cut," what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Well, the Petkovci Dam is constructed of rubble, quarried lumps of rock maybe as big as this desk, angular.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So man cut through a quarry is what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. Not quarried into rectangular blocks but blasted and cut up into a form which forms a rubble stabilising wall for the dam.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey and Professor, I would like to ask you to pause between question and answer. As you are using the same language, there are some problems with the record otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. That's my fault.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And can you briefly tell us about a secondary site along Cancari Road that you were able to connect to the primary site of Kozluk.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. You're referring to Cancari 3 is the name -- number we gave to the grave you're asking about. We had -- we assumed it was a secondary grave because it appeared on aerial imagery from October 1995. The first thing we do at a site is to scrape the surface to define whether there is a grave there and exactly where it is, to see the edges. As we were scraping the surface, some hundreds if not thousands of pieces of broken green glass bottles were found, including some with the -- although they were broken, with their crown seals on the top, and we also found a great thick pile of labels from the Kozluk Bottling Factory. Such glass was not to be found in this valley. I mean, it was not a result of a rubbish dump. It was found -- the glass was found only in what later turned out to be a mass grave, and so I formed the opinion that the bodies that were in the secondary grave must have come from a site which was strewn with broken bottle glass. And since the name "Kozluk" was on the labels, I told ICTY -- I told the investigators that I thought there was a primary grave which was, in fact, unknown at that time at Kozluk. And in -- I think it was 30 or 40 kilometres away from the secondary grave. And then later that year, I went -- or late -- after I'd reported this find, I went with the investigators to Kozluk, went behind the bottling factory, and we found a place where there were human remains lying on the surface. And in 1999, I and my team went to Kozluk and found the source of the bodies. There were still some 300 or so left in part of the primary grave that hadn't been interfered with, and we exhumed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you see any green glass in this area where you exhumed the grave?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: The area was covered with green glass.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And was there a bottle factory close by?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: There was a bottle factory close by. I think there must have been some accident in the bottling factory, since there was just one type of bottle which was broken up into thousands of -- one type of bottle that had been broken up into thousands of fragments. So it was a specific case of the transfer of evidence from a primary grave to a secondary grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, thank you for those few examples. I know you and I could talk for days on this topic, but let me go to something else. In your testimony last time, you acknowledged that when you were doing the work for the ICTY, you had not had the experience of exhuming graves that contained battle casualties. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, I hadn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, you had exhumed a grave in the Ukraine from World War II; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, a massacre of Jews in 19 -- of about 550 Jews by a [indiscernible] contingent in 1942.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But that was --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: They had been shot in the back of the head. Not battle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, you have -- have you, since your last testimony, gained any experience in exhuming graves containing battle casualties?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. Last year, I worked for -- as a senior forensic adviser for a company called Oxford Archaeology. It had a contract to exhume eight pits in Frommel, which is just across the border from Belgium, near Lille. And in 1916, an Australian contingent made an attack on German machine-gun posts and well over a thousand Australians were killed that night. They were then -- those that made their way into the German trenches in the course of the battle or were killed immediately in front of the German trenches were then buried by the Germans in -- they dug eight graves, but they only used five. And Oxford Archaeology was responsible for removing these bodies that were buried in the course of battle, and they've now been reburied in a war cemetery at Frommel. Now, I was there at the beginning of this work, and I've subsequently studied the disposition of these bodies in the mass graves. I wasn't part of the exhumation team, as such, but I have now had experience of war graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We know from your prior testimony that many of the graves you saw in Bosnia, the bodies were all mixed up or torn apart, and so that's largely what you're viewing as you're doing your exhumation work. How about this grave in Belgium?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: We know from the Bavarian Regiment or Brigade -- I'm not good on military terms. We know from the Bavarian records that the Germans were told to bury these people with respect, and what we found in the five pits were that the bodies were laid side by side, in two layers. Not laid out with complete -- as you would be in a coffin, but that would be, in my opinion, due to the effects of rigidity in the body, because they were buried within a week of being killed. So they were -- yes, they were respectfully arranged.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, as you recall, last trial quite a bit of the cross-examination was spent on the possibility of battle casualties and your experience in this regard. Does your experience with the grave in Belgium assist you in your overall view of your work? Does it cause you to change any opinions of what you had done in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: No, it hasn't caused me to change opinions, but I think I would be very careful in -- I would not like to generalise from the Fromel graves as to what war graves, in general, look like. But that they contain people in uniform and with military accoutrements, that we certainly saw at Frommel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were there any identifications able to be made of the Australians in the Frommel grave?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. There were some British there, and they think out of the 250, probably 30 or so were British. But the Australian Department of Defence set up a large DNA programme, inviting relatives who knew that they had lost predecessors of their family at Frommel, to volunteer swabs for DNA analysis. And the project was able to identify -- after this mass application of DNA, was able to identify 96 out of the 250 individuals that we recovered, and most of those were identified by DNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And have you had a chance to look at or briefly review the DNA studies that have been done, well, relatively recently by the ICMP regarding the graves that you exhumed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: That's out of my field, and I wouldn't care to answer questions on that. And I certainly haven't reviewed it, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. The science of DNA that was able to identify people, for example, from the Frommel grave, was that something that you had at all anticipated having at your finger-tips in 1998, 1999, 2000 when you were doing your work?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: No, I think that it probably was unprecedented at that time. I would not have thought that it was going to be applied, but it wouldn't have been up to me to do that, anyway. But I've not heard of mass DNA work on that scale.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Professor Wright. I think that gives us a foundation for the cross-examination. I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. McCloskey. Mr. Tolimir, now it's your turn with your cross-examination. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to greet everybody in the courtroom. I would like to wish Mr. Wright a good afternoon. May there be peace in this house, and may the divine providence bring justice not according to my wishes but according to God's will. Can we look at this witness's CV, please. This is Exhibit P890, and we will look at page 1. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It says here that you are an associate of the Centre for Comparative Studies on Genocide. My question is: Are you able to describe briefly where the institute is, what topics does it deal with, and what is your role in this institute? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. That is really an outdated entry. The -- I think that the Centre for Comparative Genocide Studies at Macquarie University has closed down, but I was closely associated with them. Macquarie University is in Sydney. I was closely associated with them when I was working on the Holocaust material. They're interested primarily in the Jewish Holocaust, and I worked with them then at Macquarie University. But I have no link with them for the Bosnian work.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I would like to ask you to tell us if you were an associate of that centre before you were engaged on the exhumations of mass graves in Bosnia and Herzegovina or not. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I find that hard to remember now, but I think the answer is, yes, I was associated with that centre before I was contacted by ICTY. I think the work was done mainly in 1995, but my memory is bad on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Can you please tell us now this: You, as a member of the Medical Doctors Group for Human Rights that is headquartered in Boston, were you a member of that group, in fact, and were you engaged on the activities -- on the exhumation of mass graves in Bosnia and Herzegovina precisely because you were a member of that group? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I was listed in that group's list of experts, but they never asked me to do any work for them, and I never have done any work for them. So they didn't ask me to do work in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. My next question is: During the work on the exhumations, were you faced with any kind of problem of a logistical nature? And if so, could you tell us what kind of a problem it was, and when did you have to face it? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Well, my first reply would be that all these mass graves yield logistical problems that have to be solved, but I can't think of a particular problem. For instance -- can I give one example to show what I would regard as a problem? At the Petkovci Dam, the earth-moving equipment that we had was totally inadequate for removing large rocks, and we had to delay the work until we could hire an excavator from Tuzla and bring it across. Is that the sort of question, General Tolimir, you -- logistical question you're asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, that's mostly what I was thinking of. And now can you please tell us, in your work, were you exposed to any kind of pressure of any type; for example, that something had to be completed within a certain time-frame or that you had to apply a certain method that you disagreed with in the exhumation process? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: As to the first question of time, yes, we had to complete the work within the scheduled period because of the security that we were being provided with by SFOR. That didn't, however, in my view, compromise any of the work. We were always finished within the time to my satisfaction. The second question was -- can you just repeat the second question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were there cases when you had to apply a particular method in your work that you did not agree with but it was imposed on you by others? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, I understand what you're asking. No, my view was that I was contracted by the ICTY as -- to do the work according to what I regarded as suitable standards. I had discussions at times with the investigators about the direction of the work, but at no time did I have pressure put on me, other than to work faster. But I didn't work faster, or my team didn't work faster, so in my view, my professional view, none of the work that we did was compromised by pressure put on me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Professor. Can we now look at Exhibit P890. P890, in e-court. Can we look at page 2 in the English?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Mindua has a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness -- I'm sorry for interrupting the Defence. When I look at your resume, Witness, you were in the Royal Air Force from 1954 to 1956?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why do you say on the record, on page 15, line 15, that you don't know the military term which has been mentioned? Do you know the difference between a regiment and a brigade, when you talked about the German Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what -- whether the Bavarian group in 1916 was a regiment, or a brigade, or how -- what it would have called itself. I haven't studied the history of that aspect of the German Army. I would -- and in the British Air Force, we don't -- we didn't use the words "regiment" and "brigade," so far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Can we now look at P890, page 2 in the English. Yes, this is this same document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, you can see it on your screen. Can you please -- thank you. Can you please clarify for us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... in B/C/S also, the second page, please. Sorry. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you please clarify for us your role in the process of exhumations conducted in the area of Bosnia and Herzegovina? It says here you were the director of exhumations of mass graves in Serniki, the Ukraine, and that you were an archaeologist in your work on the exhumations in the former Yugoslavia, so can you please explain to us the difference between these two functions? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I think there isn't a difference between the two functions. The word "director" and my title, which was chief archaeologist, are not in disagreement with each other. It indicates that -- in both cases, that I was in charge of the exhumations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you the person in charge both in the Ukraine and in Bosnia and Herzegovina? Is that something that we can conclude from your answer or not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, I had the same role in both the Ukraine and in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, can you please tell us, who was your boss? Who was the leader of the exhumation team during your work there in Bosnia and Herzegovina? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I was the leader of the exhumation team. I was in charge of the exhumations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have a superior above you, other than the representatives of the International Criminal Tribunal who engaged you on this work?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I was answerable to the chief of operations, who was based in The Hague. I think that's the title. And the person who occupied that position changed from time to time. That was the person who could hire me or fire me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Can you please tell us whether this chief of operations, who had this role of a boss, could issue binding instructions to you in your work in Bosnia and Herzegovina and directives for your work? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Only in a very general sense of where I was supposed to go, because they needed to provide the support. But I was not required to send in reports to this person, and I never received instructions about how I should carry out the work. But the chief of operations would come down periodically and talk to me about the work, but not to tell me what to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you were not obliged to submit reports or report back to the chief of operations, were you obliged to report back to anyone else or to, as it were, accept corrections in your further work? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: No, I was not asked to make corrections, if that's what you mean, to my work. I regarded myself as a contracted forensic archaeologist, and I would -- if I had found that my work was being interfered with, then I would have resigned. I only had to give five days' notice. I was not interfered with in the Ukraine. I was not interfered with in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You understood me correctly. I just wanted to get the answer to my question whether there was any kind of interference in the actual procedure, and the answer was, No, nobody interfered in the actual exhumation procedure. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Can I just clarify? Nobody -- we would have discussed various ways of doing things, but my view was the one that would always carry. I said what I was doing. I was urged, at times, to work faster. If that -- perhaps you might say that's interference, but it was not telling me how to do the work. But I pointed out that the recovery of the bodies with the evidence required us to work at the speed we were working, and that was accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor, for this explanation. Can you please tell us, who was the chief investigator in this period at The Hague Tribunal, and what was his role in the actual procedure of exhumations? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I just need some clarification, I think, of titles here. The chief investigator was, I think, John Ralston at the time, but he was not concerned with the field-work. The head of investigations was somebody called John Ralston. But if you mean the particular case that I was working on while I was working at the graves, the Srebrenica case, then that was Mr. Jean Ruez. He was the investigator, local investigator.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Your understanding was correct, I meant Mr. Jean-Rene Ruez. That's who I had in mind, and I wanted you to tell me what sort of role he had in the process of exhumations. If you could tell the Trial Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Mr. Jean-Rene Ruez never took part in the exhumations. He would come and visit the site, but he was not a member of the exhumation team. The team consisted of about 10 experts. He wasn't an -- he wasn't taking part in the exhumations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does this mean that he had no influence whatsoever on the very process of exhumations? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Well, no. He respected me as an expert, and he had a role, I suppose, because he must have decided, in part, which of the graves we should excavate, though ultimately it was left to me to decide whether the exhumation was feasible. I mean, I had a choice. But on the day-to-day activities of how we did the work, no, he had no role to play. He was, as I -- in my opinion, a visitor to the site. I did not adjust my work because of what he told me to do. He did not interfere in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Did the chief investigator, in this case it was Mr. Jean-Rene Ruez, issue to you any sort of a binding instruction relating to your work in the exhumations? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: No, absolutely not, he didn't issue any instructions to me. I wouldn't have accepted instructions from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you were hired to work at several localities, who would replace you at one site when you attended to another? What can you tell us in that respect? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I never worked at more than one site at a time. I had a team, and we worked at one site at a time. In the year 2000, when I took some leave in the middle of the work, then Mr. Fredy Peccerelli, from Guatemala, was acting chief archaeologist, but the team was still working on one grave at a time, never more than one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this mean that you would not start work on a grave-site before work on another grave-site was completed, in your view? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, we didn't start exhuming a new grave before we knew we had exhumed all the bodies from a previous grave. The only exception to this, but it's not really an exception to what I said about not exhuming until we'd finished, but we did probe some of the suspect secondary graves. We did test to see whether they had bodies, but we didn't exhume them. And I would test these graves while the team was doing the exhumations, but we never did more than one exhumation at a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If my understanding is correct -- or, rather, I'll put my question, and you'll make that conclusion yourself. So you were also charged with detecting graves. You were charged with co-ordinating the process of exhumations, as you say, not more than at one site at a time. And did this work also include analysis of artefacts retrieved from a grave-site? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Not analysis of artefacts, no. Observation of -- an observation of what kind of artefacts we had and an entry in the log was made, but we didn't study the artefacts, nor did we study the bodies. We made some observations on the bodies and some observations on the artefacts, and -- because we had to enter these observations into our log, into our register. But we didn't spend time studying them. We took -- one special thing we did was -- I suppose you could say "study," in a sense, but it would require a more detailed study, in the end, but when we found wallets, we would open up the wallet to reveal the -- to reveal both sides, and often a wallet will contain an immediately visible photograph of the person who owns the wallet -- or at least a photograph of a person, which one assumes owns the wallet, and we would take a photograph of that, because there's a risk, once the pictures have been exposed to the air again, to oxygen, that they will deteriorate. And, therefore, if we left that -- if we left everything to the people working at the morgue, they might have defective and damaged documents. So we took those pictures, and we also had with us the Red Cross missing persons register. I don't know the exact title, but it was a list of names and where people were last seen. And we would look them up to see if they were on that register. And I do, in my reports, to give a general context to what we were finding, point out that many of the names are in the Red Cross register. That was a bit of study, but not a final study. We were too pressed for time and we didn't have the expertise to study everything as it came out of the ground. We left that to the investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I didn't want to interrupt you. My question wasn't about the way in which the analysis was made, but how you would secure the process of exhuming, including artefacts themselves. That's what my question had to do with. Maybe it was misinterpreted. So I imagine you wouldn't have time to deal with security, itself. Did you have somebody else doing that for you there? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Do you mean the security of the bodies and artefacts, to make certain that no one tampered with them, or do you mean of our own security, physical security, which was provided by SFOR? Which are you asking?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. No, no, I was misinterpreted, my assistant told me. I meant security of bodies and artefacts, the work, meaning securing bodies and artefacts for the purposes of subsequent study. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: That was my first interpretation of what you were asking. We had at all the sites a police officer who was an expert in chain of custody, as it's called, and he would enter these objects into a log and they'd be put in a sealed bag, and that sealed bag would be put into a locked van in which there were both bodies and artefacts, and it was chilled to prevent deterioration both of the bodies and of the artefacts. So there was a scene-of-crime officer who was responsible for the security of the bodies and for the security of the artefacts, and they were kept in a locked -- a locked van.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you responsible for the entire process and for the synchronisation of the entire process, as you've just explained to us? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, I -- I was -- took advice from the scene-of-crime officer as to what the appropriate sequence of events was, but -- but if I had -- if I saw that that process was not being carried out, I suppose I would have had to interfere. But I didn't interfere with the scene-of-crime officers. They were doing their work, so far as I could see, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you explain this by reference to an example, to make it clearer to us? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. Let us suppose we're looking in the grave, and an archaeologist reports that he or she has found a wallet; not with a body but just a wallet. Then the position of that wallet would be -- to give you an example, the position of that wallet would be recorded by the surveyor, the scene-of-crime officer would assign a reference number to that wallet -- and in our logs they begin with "A" for "Artefact." They would assign the letter A for "Artefact." The senior crime officer would then take possession of this object and put it into a bag, enter the details into the log, and then it would be put in the van that was kept locked. And then all those -- all the bodies and all the objects were sent down to the morgue in Visoko in this locked van. So it's a case of the scene-of-crime officer allocating a number, the surveyor surveying where this object is found -- I think I missed out the photographer. The photographer takes a picture of the object before it's moved, and then the scene-of-crime officer takes possession of the object, enters it into the log, and then puts it in a secure place. And then there's an official hand-over of material periodically to the morgue in Visoko.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor, for this example. Can you give us an illustration of where you realised that something had went wrong? In this instance, you refer to a wallet that you retrieved which you didn't know who it belonged to. And was there a an example where something had gone wrong, that you encountered a difficulty?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I think I'll have to ask you, General Tolimir, to be a bit more specific about what you mean by "something had gone wrong." I don't quite understand what you mean by that. What kind of thing has gone wrong?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll make myself clear. You've just given us an example of how work was supposed to be done. Now, in your work, was there a situation where something was done improperly and it had to be remedied so that the procedure could be finished in a proper way, something that would have a bearing on your work? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I can't remember any mistake that was made that was of any consequence to the integrity of the evidence. There may have been some minor breaches of the protocols. And, incidentally, the protocols were given to all the workers at the site, and they are in my reports. I don't know of a systematic, that is, long-lasting, breach of those protocols or -- and I can't remember any mistake which at the time I thought was of any consequence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Can you tell me now, was it your responsibility - and if it wasn't yours, whose was it - to establish the cause and manner of death of an individual found in a grave? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: The responsibility for establishing the cause and manner of death was done not at the site. It was done by the anthropologist and pathologist in the morgue. Nevertheless, I was able to see on many occasions -- for instance, if someone has a bullet through their head, I, not as an expert, will assume that that is the cause of death, and I might even write it in my notes, but I wouldn't have established it in the strict -- in the strict sense. That wasn't my job.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I asked you this bearing in mind the example you gave in your examination-in-chief, where you established that the individuals were murdered, killed, because they had ligatures and blindfolds, and it had to do with whether this was established at the site or whether it was established subsequently in the morgue. But you've understood my question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, was that a question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. No, I'm happy with the answer the professor gave. I just said why I put this question, because it had to do with what he said in the direct examination. And if he has comments on it, very well. If not, that's fine also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No explanation needed. I just wanted to ask you if that was a question. You said, No, and then I can say: Carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us, did you write reports and analyses in the course of exhumations or did you write only the reports that were adduced here as evidence before this Court? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I wrote no reports in the course of the work. We -- we filled out the logs for each item, and they would have been handed over to the morgue, but I did not write interim reports, except in the one case of that Grave L at Glogova. That's my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have your comments in relation to the question I'm about to put to you? The reports that were presented here and admitted into evidence, what was the basis on which you wrote them? Were those notes, analyses that you made back in the relevant time in the course of exhumations, or were there any other bases for the reports that were presented here? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I know what you mean. Yes, well, in the course of being at the site, I kept my own personal notes about the work, and they assisted me in writing up the reports. Together with the photographs and the logs, I was able to write up my reports. My reports are fairly brief, and they really are an explanation, if you like, for the photographs that were taken and the -- and the logs, themselves. There were body sheets which I -- which were -- of which I give an illustration, I think, in most of the reports, which were filled out by my team, and I had those available to me when I wrote my reports, but there were no -- there were no other documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And in each and every report of yours, there exists a protocol on the procedure of exhumations. Please tell me, is there one protocol which applied to each and every exhumation carried out or were there different protocols applying to different exhumations? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, the answer to your question is yes. There were different protocols. They evolved in the light of what we saw as the needs, so that they do differ slightly from year to year. And the final protocol that I wrote and which the team had to study, the final protocol was the one we used at Glogova in the year 2000. There are slight differences. We would -- if I could just explain. We set ourselves in the -- at the start of the work, over-ambitiously, we wanted to photograph every shell case that we found. At the end of the work, we were recording them, but we were not photographing each shell case. Those sorts of differences that would allow us to get the work accomplished without compromising the quality of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. The exhumation procedure was envisaged ahead of work, was it not, but were there modifications made as the work progressed, and can you give us examples? Thank you. Let me put it simply: Were there instances where one had to depart from the protocol in the process of exhumation, or modify it? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: We made modifications to the procedure of exhumation; that is, strictly speaking, the removal of the bodies, but I'm not sure -- I can't remember that these were modifications of the protocols. But if I can just explain. The general procedure is to remove a body that has soft tissue as soon as possible, because it decomposes and there's loss of evidence once it's re-exposed to oxygen. So they tended to be removed one at a time, and we were able to survey the bodies -- the body that we removed so we would afterwards know its relationship to other bodies in the grave. At Kozluk, we made a change in one place, where we decided that we were looking at a single layer of bodies lying on a surface. About 15 bodies were emerging, and we thought that this should be left -- they should be left on this surface for photography to show what the view would have been like before they were covered up. Now, I have to say, without consulting the protocols, I couldn't say whether that was a breach of the protocols or a change in the protocols. I don't think so. But it was the only change to the general rule that you remove the bodies when you find them and work out their relationship to each other from the three-dimensional survey that we did. But at Kozluk, in one area we left the bodies exposed. We did uncover more than one without removing the previous ones. But that's the only change I can think of.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My legal assistant says that on page 31, you said "15 bodies," and the transcript states "50." Line 21.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: That can't be. Not -- the particular site -- area I'm talking about is Kozluk, and you'd need to direct me to my report on Kozluk because it's only a matter of 15, 1-5, bodies. Where in the transcript is this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It was an interpretation problem, and it's now corrected. Thank you. Can we now call up Exhibit P872 in e-court. It's Mr. Wright's report on the exhumations carried out in Eastern Bosnia in 1998, which is dated the 12th of May, 1999. You'll be able to see it here in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question has to do with the cover page. The exhumations were conducted in 1998, as the heading, or as the title states. Now, at the bottom, the date is the 12th of May, 1999. This is the date when the report was filed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: It was the date that I submitted the report to the -- to ICTY. That was my date, when I finished it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there anything else that would speak as to the difference when the exhumations were carried out and the subsequent five-month period when the actual report was submitted? Is there any other reason for this, other than the formal reasons; the time required for the report to be typed and so on? What would be the reason for the submission of the report five months later?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I can't remember in detail why. I came to ICTY in, I think, February 1999 to examine the photographs and to go through the logs. I then went back to Sydney, where I finished my report. I can't remember what else I was doing at that time, but I can't think of any special reason for the interval of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us, since you worked in the Ukraine, was there the specific situation there as well that you wrote the report some months or years later, after the fact? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Well, I've never written reports some years after the fact, General Tolimir, but this -- one reason I can -- a specific reason which now comes to my mind is that we were unable to estimate exactly, at the excavation, how many bodies there were in each grave. That work was done at the morgue, and it was done after we'd completed our work. And you will notice that I include in my report estimates of the number of bodies that I received from the morgue. That would have been one reason why I couldn't have hurried to write my report, because I would -- wanted to wait until the work at the morgue was completed. Other than that, I can't comment further. I don't remember ICTY telling me to get on with it. They were satisfied with the report being received in May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think we need the first break now. The tapes must be rewound, and we -- on technical reasons, we must have a break now. We will resume a quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My next question is: The content of the report you wrote on the Ukraine matters, were they presented in a different way than the material that you presented on the results of your work in Bosnia and Herzegovina or did you present the material in both reports in the same way? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: In the case of the Ukraine, my report was in the form of a statement. It was very brief and not like the reports that I have presented to ICTY. The Ukrainian reports were two- or three-page statements of the basic observations that I've made, so there was a difference.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Professor. Can we now look at page 8 of this document in the Serbian and page 7 in the English, for illustration purposes. This is the document that we already are looking at in the e-court. Thank you. Page 7 in the English, please. Thank you. And page 6 in the Serbian version, please. Page 8 in the English, can we look at that, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: If you have the page in the English, perhaps you can explain this term "probed graves." If you can explain what that means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, we don't have it. And I think now we have a certain page 8, but it is not corresponding to the other one, I suppose, to the B/C/S page. We need the correct reference. Otherwise, the witness can't comment on that. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as Mr. Tolimir said in the beginning, it's page 8 in the Serbian. It was on the screen in the very beginning. Yes, this is the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And now we can see where you're talking about, for example, in paragraph CR01, where you say: "Probed on the 16th of June, 1998." Are you able to explain to us what it means, to probe a grave? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I understand your question, General Tolimir. Let me first say that we exhumed seven graves. But on the aerial images that we had, there was disturbed soil in several other places, and in 21 of those places we were able to find the outlines of a grave, and we removed soil from that grave until we had at least -- we had the remains of at least two people, and they were generally near the top. And then we call that "probing." It's not the sticking in of a probe, but it's the testing by means of using -- by using the mechanical excavator to see whether this disturbed ground has bodies in it, and not just one, but more than -- two or more. But we didn't remove them. We filled the holes that we had made. We filled them up with soil, and all of those disturbed patches of soil in which we found bodies are listed in this report that I wrote in 1999. That's -- is that an adequate answer for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm satisfied with the answer. I just want to ask you: When you are probing a grave, is it possible that you would injure or disturb body parts? Perhaps you can later provide exact definitions as I go on putting questions to you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. The -- first of all, I was always there, so that I would immediately see if the backhoe was disturbing clothes. Normally, you find clothes before you find the body. There is a risk of damage, not big damage, but of breaking a bone in that process. But the operator of the backhoe was extremely experienced. He could tell by the feel of the bucket in the soil whether he was touching anything hard or whether he was just touching soil. So I would say, in general, we did not break things, certainly not seriously.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Professor. Can we now look at page 17 in the Serbian of this document, and page 15 in the English. We are interested in a definition of "body parts."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And while we're waiting for this to show up, Professor, if you would just tell us whose responsibility it was to establish the minimum number of bodies in a grave. Was this assessment made at the scene or was this something that was determined in a different way?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: In answering that, I just want to explain my own experience at -- in the Ukraine. In the Ukraine, we could tell exactly how many bodies there were. The bodies were in position -- all the bones were in position because they were undisturbed. But when I had to deal with the graves in Bosnia, we kept finding a leg which was not connected to any other part of the body, a foot in a shoe. In particular, at these secondary graves, we had problems in defining how many individuals we had, and we didn't even attempt to come up with a number because of the risks of double-counting individuals when they were broken up. So that process of estimating the number of individuals was left to the people who studied the remains in the morgue. I had a rough idea of how many bodies there might be in each grave, but I haven't used those estimates. I have used, in my report, numbers that I was given after the analysis had been completed at the morgue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since each part of the body - an arm, a leg - is defined as "the body," is it then the case that after the examinations at the morgue, it was definitely established what it means to have the whole body? Are individual parts also marked as body parts when they're excavated, and then in the morgue it is established what goes with what? My question actually is: Are body parts that were found, individual body parts, also given marks or numbers and then sent to the morgue as bodies? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: No. We had a protocol established, and it's mentioned, for the various sites, that we have three categories when we make an entry into the log. We have a body, that is, so many remains of that individual are present that we know we're dealing with an individual, and we're not going to -- well, there is an individual there because so much is present. But then we have in our logs "body parts," which we used the initials "BP," and that would be a leg or a forearm, but we wouldn't -- I would not have counted those as bodies. They have a separate category, body parts, which we define in the protocols. In addition, we occasionally found just one bone, say a toe bone, and they were just not counted as body parts but were put into a bag where we just have general -- general bones that are not -- that are individual bones, not body parts. So there is -- in the log, bodies and body parts are entered separately, and then there is a bag for each site for which an isolated bone found here or there is put.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I'm asking you this because in some reports that are presented before this Tribunal, we have the case that one person was identified in a number of graves and was identified several times, and then it may appear that we're talking about two persons instead of one. Are you able to tell us something about ways to avoid something like this from happening? How did you deal with this question in order to prevent this kind of thing from happening when you are presenting your report? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Well, in my -- in my own reports -- in my own reports, that is, the ones I wrote myself, I didn't, in this document we have in front of us, offer any suggestion how many bodies there were. That was information I got from the morgue. Our responsibility was to keep separate items which were definitely -- definitely separate; that is, if we found a leg and then over here we found an arm, we didn't assume that it belonged to the same individual. We just called them body parts and sent them down to the morgue. I -- at that point, my responsibility ends, or how they operate at the morgue I can't say, because I went to the morgue on two or three occasions, but not to work there; just to make a general courtesy call. But the numbers that are in -- the numbers that are on page 32 of that report are not my counting. They are estimates that I was given by Mr. Baryabar after he had analysed the bodies at the morgue, those numbers in this table. If we can look at page 32 in the English.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at page 32, because the witness is referring to that page. So if we can see that page in e-court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Are we ready to proceed? Yes. That table, it's not my counting of bodies and body parts. Those numbers there were given to me by the morgue after they'd analysed the remains that we had sent down.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have any other comments on what is written here, since you didn't write that, that would not correspond to the manner in which you presented certain issues? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'll have to ask you to clarify that question. I don't understand the question that you're asking me as it's translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You just said that you didn't present this table the way it's been presented on this page that you asked for us to look at. So do you have your own way or your own style in which you would present this? Are there any differences in the way you would present it and the way this is presented? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I understand what you're asking now. This is my table. I went -- I spoke with Mr. Baryabar, and I said, We excavated completely these seven secondary graves, and we sent the remains to the morgue. What do you have to tell me about the number of individuals? And then I included them in that table. So -- but I can't -- I can't comment on the method by which the morgue arrived at those numbers because I wasn't part of that work. I have used numbers provided to me by the experts working in the morgue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, it's clear to me now. Before I put my next question: The term "body part," was that defined before the exhumations began or did you define this particular term at some later stage?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to remember, but I think it was probably in 1997, at the excavations of Brcko, which have nothing to do with this case, but at that site, we had this problem of graves that had been disturbed, and we were finding limbs. And I'm confident that we would have, in 1997, worked out the importance of not counting each piece as a body, but distinguishing the parts from the whole bodies. That's my memory, but I -- that we addressed that question in 1997 and then would have carried our experience over to 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. When one reads your report, it's a little bit unclear in that area that touches upon these differences, when a group of post-mortem remains is considered a complete body and when it is considered as body parts. So would you be able to explain to us that difference, when a group of remains is considered to be a complete body and when a group of remains is considered to be body parts? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I think I do deal with that question in my protocols. I have my own copy of the report here. If you could just give me a minute to see whether I included the protocols in this report. Yes, just excuse me a minute while I find it. On the English -- in the English version on page 13, I don't define what constitutes a -- I talk about a fairly complete body and I talk about body parts. A fairly complete body is one that has enough bones to be certain that another part of a body could not be confused. In other words, if I have more than half the bones, then I have a fairly complete body. If I have less than half, I run the risk of then finding the other part of that individual and saying I've got two individuals. So before we call a thing a body, we have -- we were fairly -- we were confident that we could not count that body twice, though -- and call it a second body. But I agree that I don't -- I don't, in my protocols -- I do make assumptions in the protocols that are not spelled out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Professor, if you would like to look at the screen, is that the page you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is that page 13, Your Honour? No, it's not the page I'm referring to. It's the one after -- that is the page, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm referring to that page 13 in English, where I talk about a fairly complete body and what's to be done with that. And the point about what was considered to be a fairly complete body is that a body sheet was filled out for that body, showing what parts were present. An example is given in my report on page 37 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we look at page 37, please, so that the witness can use it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it's not that page. It's the one before. That's the one.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now, here you can see that the person who excavated this body at the secondary grave Zeleni Jadar 5 has answered some questions about whether the body has been surveyed, the way in which the body lies, is it extended or is it crouched or mixed up, certain other observations, and then at the bottom you'll see a little sketch which gives a quick idea of how the body lies. And you can see, from that, what's present and what's missing. You can see it from that, but you can see it better -- and I don't have an example in my report, but you can see it better in the photographs that were taken of each of the bodies. So I would have no hesitation in saying that the person who said that this was a body on page 37 was correct. And if it had just been a leg or an arm, or even two legs, they would have been given the title of "body part," and one of these sheets would not have been filled out. So these sheets -- counting these sheets would give you a rough idea of how many bodies there were, but the final analysis, as you suggested, of what might belong to what would have to be done afterwards. What body parts might belong to this body would have to be done afterwards. And I suppose, in the question you asked me about the DNA results, that was a case where maybe a body was incompletely removed from a primary grave. We found examples in Kozluk, for instance, where an individual's left leg had been taken away when the grave was disturbed, but the rest of the body was there. There would be many explanations for why there were body parts which -- linked together, by means of DNA, but come from different sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since we have this image before us on the right-hand side, where feet and hands were circled: If you found a body without hands or feet, would you have considered the remains to be a complete body or body parts? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, I understand what you're asking. If we found a body which was complete, except that it didn't have feet or hands, we would have called it a body. We'd have called it not a complete body, but we'd have called it a body for the purposes of our entries into the log, and a sheet like this would have been filled out. If we found a hand on its own, obviously, we wouldn't have called that a body. But I can't remember a specific case of a body which had all its -- both its hands and both its feet missing, but there might have been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe has a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: At page 44 of today's transcript, lines 10 to 14, you state that: "Where an individual's left leg had been taken away when the grave was disturbed, but the rest of the body was there, there would be many explanations for why there would be body parts which -- linked together, by means of DNA, but come from different sites." Focusing specifically on this example you've given, I wonder whether you can venture to explain how only a leg would be taken away and the rest of the body was left in the grave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The site I was referring to specifically is the site of Kozluk, where the bodies were lying out on the surface, and the edge of that distribution of bodies had been cut through by a bulldozer and one leg had been taken away, and -- the bodies that were in the line of the bulldozer had been taken away, but those on the left had been left behind. So that would be one reason why, if I understand General Tolimir correctly, the DNA has shown that remains of the same individual is in more than one grave, that would be one example how that might come about. Another example of how it might come about would be that different truckloads of bodies were taken away from the primary grave to different secondary graves. That's why I said there are several possible explanations for the example that he asked me about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter 638 may be very specific to answer the Judge's question on this point. Of course, I could bring it up in redirect, but I'm hoping I won't have any redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: At this point in time, the answer was sufficient enough. Thank you very much. Carry on, please, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Professor, in order for us to fully understand how you treated body parts and a whole body, please look at paragraph 2, where, amongst other things, it is said that an excavator would scoop up bodies. That's page 18 in Serbian and 15 in English. Thank you. Thank you. I will be mindful of having to speak slowly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: We're looking at page 14 in the English, not 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: That's right. We were looking for page 15 in English and page 17 in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please, page 15 --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We've had it on our screens once before. Thank you, we have it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is the section "Definition of Body Parts."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
