utterances.text: We don't have it in English yet. Thank you. Now it's page 15.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us look at paragraph 2 now, where it is stated -- you state: "A decision had to be made on how to remove, spatially record, and label these disarticulated parts. To aid the exhumation work, the parts were therefore given the name 'body part.' The definition of any particular body part was made by the individual excavator."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Based on what I've just read, I'd like you to answer this: What -- how do you define a retrieved body part? What do you imply by it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I don't imply anything in terms of how it got into that state. Merely by calling it a body part I'm not coming up with any explanation. It's an empirical observation that here is the bones of a leg, and we look around and there's no pelvis, there's no other body to which it can belong. Now, how it got into that state is a -- is a secondary question that needs to be explained, I agree. But we define a body part in an empirical -- in an observational way, not interpreting how it got into that state. So a leg is a leg, and that's a body part. It sometimes happened that we did subsequently think that a body a little bit further away which is missing a leg probably -- that the leg belonged to that body, but we would not have then -- we'd have left that to the morgue to decide. And I did provide the morgue with survey data that would assist them in the three-dimensional space of the grave to work out, well, which pelvis is closest to this leg in three-dimensional space within the grave. That might help speed up their process of reconstruction of whole bodies, but to call it a body part is not to explain how it got into that state. It just is an isolated part of the body that is found.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. A moment ago, in answer to Her Honour Judge Nyambe's question, you said how it was possible that a body part such as a foot would be -- would disappear as a body part because it would be dismembered from the rest of the body by an excavator. Since these bodies lay on the surface for several months -- Mr. Ruez, himself, testified that he had found 600 bodies lying on the surface unprotected and which had been there for several months. Now, if an animal were to take a body part, how would that be defined in the morgue? In what way would you be able to complete the identification process of a body? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey. Before you answer, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is a complete misstatement of the evidence. There are -- there is nothing in the record, nor Mr. Ruez's testimony, regarding any bodies from the mass graves associated with any of the work of Professor Wright where the bodies were thought to be on the surface for that long. So this has nothing to do with this witness's testimony, and yet he, of course, can't know that because he's not party to Mr. Ruez's testimony. Therefore, I object to the misstatement and mis-characterisation of the evidence, as it would not provide us any answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Taking it into account, the statement and the objection of Mr. McCloskey, are you able to answer the core of the question of Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There's a misunderstanding of my previous statement. The bodies that I was talking about at Kozluk were found on a surface, but that surface was buried under soil. The floor of this court is a surface, and things can lie on the surface. But then in the case of Kozluk, they had all been covered up with soil, and we had to excavate before we found that surface. That's what I meant. They had not been exposed to predators or the elements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Professor, it was not my intention to put provocative questions or ill-intentional questions. I wanted to learn from you, as a professor, how you would complete an identification process of a body missing body parts which could not be found on the site for whatever reasons. Maybe they were taken away by animals. I mentioned Mr. Ruez because he said that he found 600 victims in Kamenica and they were unprotected. They could have been taken away, their body parts, by either domestic animals or wild animals. So how would the identification process of an individual be completed, and how would this be formulated in a report after the analysis you made and the analysis the offices in the morgue made? So my -- I was well-intentioned in putting this question, because we have encountered such problems in this courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: No, I understand, General Tolimir, and I think there was a misunderstanding, because in English we use the words "the" and "a," and I said they were found, at Kozluk, on a surface, and that's a different meaning from "the surface" in English. It may be that something was lost. I know a bit of Russian and I know that there's often confusion because in Russian there isn't the word "the" and not the word "a" and it's possible that's where the confusion arose. But I had no difficulty in interpreting this site at Kozluk, which is not part of this report, as having -- that the movement -- the moving away of the leg was due to machinery cutting through the bodies, not that a predator could have got at the site. In fact, I don't remember -- the only site where bodies were very close to the surface, that I saw, was at Ravnice, but I wasn't responsible, I wasn't managing that work, but they were found very close to the surface. But we did not see evidence of chewing of the bones. And given the stratification at the site, we got clear evidence that as soon as the bodies had been put into the graves, they were covered up with soil, so not subsequently disturbed by predators, with one -- I think one exception, that something had burrowed into the bones in a very limited area in Cancari Road 3, a bone had been pulled up to the surface, but the soil was covering the rest of the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. The question I put to you did not refer to your report. I was merely presenting you with an example. I didn't refer to your report. I wanted your expert opinion as to how one would proceed when a body is found on the surface with some body parts missing, and I merely wanted to know how this would be treated as an occurrence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Is that a question, General Tolimir, to ask how I would treat a body that was on the surface?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, that's my question. How would this be treated in a report that we would read here in the courtroom, or would this pose difficulties in the final identification, causing it to last for 15 or 16 years before the relevant body parts were found? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Bodies that are left on the surface certainly pose problems for forensic investigators, because animals like foxes, often wild cats, and birds will pull the bodies around, and so that material will be distributed over a big area. But I never met bodies on the surface. In my work, the bodies were always buried.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Tell us, please, when it comes to the graves, themselves, to what extent does the pressure exerted by soil -- as there would be the natural depositing of soil, as well as perhaps machinery driving across the surface, to what extent would that have an impact on the damage inflicted on the bodies? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Well, pressure of soil and pressure of vehicles going across a site might well cause damage to the bodies, but not disassociation. The parts of the body would remain undisturbed, but there might be compression of the rib cage and so the ribs would be broken. There's often compression of the skull so that the skull is distorted. But all the bits will be there, unlike the case where bones are on the surface and a fox has pulled the bones apart. Provided they're in place, the pressure of the soil, the pressure of other bodies, will cause compression, but not disarticulation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You have already said that the bodies and artefacts retrieved in the graves could not have been exposed to considerable damage by the earth-moving machinery and the probing that had been done. You said that damage caused through these activities was minimal. Was there any damage which could have had a decisive bearing on the ultimate identification process?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: If you mean damage caused by the exhumation team -- if you mean damage caused by the exhumation team, then there would be a very small amount of damage. They worked with trowels and brushes to expose the bones. The main problem to identification, the main -- identification of what is a body, I mean, the main problem was caused by the fact that the secondary graves contained bodies that had been brought from somewhere else, and in the course of their excavation as a primary grave, the transporting of them to the secondary grave, and the dumping of them in the secondary grave, there was considerable disarticulation of individual skeletons, and certainly the clarity of the analysis that could be done is affected by that. If the bodies are -- for instance, when I worked in the Ukraine, the bodies had never been disturbed since 1942. They were lying exactly as they died. The pathologist didn't even need -- in the case of most of the 550 bodies that we uncovered, the pathologist could work on the site, and then they were not -- the remains were then reburied. So in primary graves that are not disturbed, there's very little loss of evidence and association, but obviously in secondary graves there will be varying degrees of disarticulation of the bodies, though the methods used in the morgue for coming up with what's known as counting the minimum number of individuals, that method tries to minimise the double-counting of individuals and so on. It's a technique used. Counting the most frequently-occurring bone and saying that is the minimum number of individuals, that seeks to alleviate the problem of the secondary graves that contain bodies and body parts. But I didn't do that. That's what they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, if it is presented through reports adduced here that such and such a number of victims or mortal remains were identified, so if that's established in these reports, that there was such and such a number of remains, following your analysis, and if it is established, once the analysis is done in the morgue, that the number of individuals involved is different, how is this addressed, and how is it established where the difference in these numbers originated from, if you understand what I'm asking you? If not, I'll put my question again.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: No, I understand what you're asking me, General Tolimir. I think the main point I would make is I did not establish the number of bodies or use any estimate that we came up with in the field. I had an idea of how many bodies there might be, but that doesn't figure in my reports and I've never tendered it officially. The numbers in my reports from the secondary graves, and the primary graves, for that matter, in other reports, are derived from the estimates made by the morgue, because it was only in Kozluk that I could say, in the case of about 300 bodies, that we could just count them as you would count individual corpses on the ground, because they hadn't been in the main part of the Kozluk site, which was a primary grave disturbed. But for the secondary graves, I don't try anywhere in my report to come up with an estimate, so there can't be any discrepancy between any numbers I report and any numbers that the morgue reports, because I've used only the information derived from the morgue after their analysis. I have never presented an analysis of the number of individuals, except for what the morgue has told me, for that table that we looked at.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. In the course of exhumations of all the artefacts you retrieved, was anything discarded, such as pieces of clothing or pieces of broken bottles that you referred to, or was everything sent on for analysis?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: In the case of the dam site, where there were no complete bodies, there were just isolated body parts, there were also lots of scattered items of clothing in the re-filling of the disturbed grave, and I -- we looked at them from the point of view of keeping those which might assist with the personal identification of the person, and I think there we did discard some. But in the graves that are listed in that table, no, we would have kept the clothes and sent them down. By "personal identification," I mean that a sweater which has been hand-knitted and is found with a body, it might well be that a wife or a mother would recognise that sweater, but if it was just in the filling of the grave, on its own, a pair of jeans, commercially-made clothing, I think in the case of Kozluk we just put them all together. I can't remember if we discarded them or not. But certainly for the graves we're talking about, the seven -- the seven exhumed secondary graves, we would have sent the material down to the morgue even if we found a bit of clothing that wasn't being worn, as it were, by a body --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. For the record, tell us what you did with the material that you put in a heap, that you did not send on for analysis. What became of that material?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: It only applied to Kozluk, and I can't remember what we did with it. I'd have to go back and consult my notes or ask other people. But I think it's true to say that we did not keep all the isolated items of clothing that were found at Kozluk, but we certainly did at all the later exhumations where we were dealing with bodies. So I can't answer your question, I'm afraid, without doing some research. You also asked -- the second part of your previous question was what we did with the other artefacts, other than clothing, such as the glass, and I think I explicitly stated in my report that we did not keep all the items of glass from Cancari 3. There were thousands of pieces of broken glass mixed up with the bodies, but we certainly kept a sample.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. This is what I'm interested in: Did you make specific notes of all the material found in a grave or did you only make note of items on the basis of which the remains could be identified? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: No, the logs, as -- I don't know if the logs have been tendered in evidence. But as you will see from the logs, there is a -- every item is recorded, with the exception of the fragments of glass. So for Cancari 3, every artefact would have been entered into the log, with the exception of the glass, and they would have been sent down to the morgue in Visoko.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And were all the members of your team instructed and trained to submit all the artefacts found in the graves for inspection or examination? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: The excavators were already, I think all of them, trained in general forensic procedures. They -- their duty was to report to the scene-of-crime officer the discovery of an artefact. And the scene-of-crime officer would collect the artefact and enter the description into the log -- would take possession of the artefact and enter it into the log. So the sequence of events was very simple, but it did require not the excavator to put the entry into the log but the scene-of-crime officer to put the entry into the log.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us if the crime technician analysed the traces on the artefacts found in the graves or did he just log them onto some list of artefacts that were found in the grave? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: The first -- the answer is the first part of your question. The scene-of-crime officer didn't analyse the artefacts beyond a simple description of what -- a wallet, or a photograph, or a coin; a simple description. That is, analysis at one very superficial level. But any subsequent analysis was done after the artefacts had been handed over to the morgue. We weren't responsible for detailed analysis. We didn't have a field laboratory that would have allowed us to look for traces of other material on the artefacts, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Can you please tell us if some artefacts were left on the scene or if they were thrown away, were not sent to the morgue or for further analysis; for example, some pieces of clothing, where maybe some samples were taken and sent on but the actual artefacts left behind? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: As I explained before, I can't remember the details, but I think that at the dam site isolated items of clothing were examined and then thrown away where they were manufactured and not associated with any bones put back in the grave. That's the only place where any artefacts were discarded. All artefacts were sent down -- recorded and sent down to the morgue, with the exception, as I explained, with the green glass at Cancari Road 3. So no one was allowed to distinguish between what might be useful artefacts and throw away the ones that they thought wouldn't be useful. They were all kept, with those exceptions as I've mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. After the entire process was completed, did you notice that there were any, perhaps, missteps that you would not repeat in any subsequent exhumation, based on that experience? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I didn't -- I don't think that in the procedures, as we developed them, there were any missteps, as you call them, that is, systematic problems with the way in which we set about the work. No, I don't think so. And the basis of the -- of the procedures that we developed, many of them are incorporated into a large textbook that's been written on mass graves, written by several people but edited by somebody called Margaret Cox, which is -- and the book is called "A Scientific Excavation of Mass Graves." And many of the procedures that we developed have been written up by people, myself included, some of them, for that book. I think that the procedures that we developed formed the foundation for the work that was done at Frommel, that World War I site where Australian soldiers were excavated. Two of the people that worked for me in Bosnia were supervisors of those graves. The forensic photographer that we had, who kept a critical visual record, he was the photographer at Frommel. One of the anthropologists that I used was responsible for the analysis of the skeletons. So people have not pointed out to us mistakes in our procedures, systematic mistakes in our procedures. On the contrary, they've been adopted by other people and published.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. My question would be this, based on what you just said: Looking at it from this perspective, is there anything that was done during the exhumations in Bosnia and Herzegovina that you would change in order to perfect that procedure in the unfortunate eventuality that these procedures would have to be repeated? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: No, definitely no change to the basic procedures. The critical -- and if I can just run through what I regard as basic procedures. That is, that the team that's doing the excavation should have experience; there should be a proper chain of custody for the artefacts; there should be three-dimensional recording of where the artefacts lie; that before a body is removed, its whole outline is clear before the body is lifted, so you don't pull bits off; that there should be a proper photographic record kept; and that notes should be passed -- notes about what you did should be passed on to the people who are at the next stage of the process, in the morgue, so they know what went with what in the grave, itself. So those basic procedures, I mean, the basic system, I wouldn't change, no. However, when you find a new grave, some of the details of the procedure will have to be changed, because, for instance, the grave might be waterlogged. None of the graves we excavated in Bosnia, except in Brcko, were waterlogged. There has to be different set of procedures if you have to keep controlling the water and the water has moved bits around. So there will be changes of -- tactical changes at a new site, but not -- I would not see the need for changes to the general strategy that I've outlined in my notes and reports. At least, no one has drawn my attention to a weak procedure that we used or one that should be changed. It may sound presumptuous of me to say that, but I do believe that the system we used and evolved is the proper forensic procedures to be used at mass graves. And many of the people who worked in Bosnia have been sought by other investigators and have taken responsible jobs in Iraq and Guatemala and were already experts in their own country, such as Argentina, on how to handle mass graves. So I was fortunate in my teams, and the teams changed with time, but I was fortunate enough to have other experts to advise me. And an excavation is run, if it's to be run well, is run with a lot of discussion about the procedures that are to be used with the other experts that are doing the work. I don't bully people into agreeing with me at the site. We have robust discussions about what the best way is of doing the work, and I had no dissenting members in the team about the procedures we were using, because they had input, themselves, into how things should be done. If that answers your question, I hope. I don't have -- I don't have a particular part of the work where I say to myself now I wish I'd done it another way. No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You've just said that there were a number of these different experts and different profiles, investigators, but now I'm going to stick to this scene-of-crime officer. Did you think that it would have been a good idea to also have a lab on the scene, a mobile lab which would be stationed close by at some location, where they would be able to perhaps examine some parts, artefacts, before they discarded them; that they could examine them for traces before definitely discarding them on a pile? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: As I've explained, there was no systematic discarding of anything, except with the two cases that I've mentioned, the dam and the green -- thousands of bottle parts. So we were not -- it would be misleading to say we were discarding things. I've outlined the two cases where material was not kept, and it was very specific -- the properties were very specific before we did. Would it have been, you asked, a good idea to have a laboratory on the site? Yes, it would, but I would always like to have everything on the site; radiocarbon, the dating laboratory, conservation laboratory. But our objects were limited. The logistics of working in Republika Srpska placed constraints on what we could have, and we had the minimum of what I regarded as essential for doing my particular job. We had that, but we didn't expand into work that could be done better under cover and over a longer period of time by people down at the morgue. But I just want to emphasise we did not have a programme of discarding things, except in those two instances I mentioned. Everything was kept.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I have one more question. How were funds secured for all of these activities that were undertaken in the field in order to identify the bodies, including DNA identification? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: My understanding is that the -- that the United Nations would get donations from countries to do the field-work that was done in Bosnia. Since all the DNA work came after I had anything to do with the project, I don't know how ICMP finances itself. I can't answer that question, because they did the DNA. So that's all I can say about the finances.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you have any information about the main donors, such as the Commission for Missing Persons? Were they able to exert any kind of influence over the overall exhumation process in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Not in my day, no, they had no influence at all. We had a strict rule that nobody from Bosnia-Herzegovina could work at the site, nobody. That even extended to the -- at the dam site, where we had to hire an excavator to remove the rocks, we provided the driver. No one who might have a bias about the interpretation of what we were finding or might be able to interfere with the site from Bosnia-Herzegovina was allowed into the -- into the site, itself. So the commission certainly never interfered with my work.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Professor. We will put the rest of the questions to other persons who were involved in the exhumation process. I would like to thank you very much for testifying on these particular matters and presenting them to us. I would like to wish you a safe return home, and I would like to thank you again for assisting us with your answers. Mr. President, these are all the questions that I have for this witness. I have completed my cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tolimir. Mr. McCloskey, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just very briefly. Could we pull up 65 ter 638. And this is a -- this will be a photograph that may take a little longer to come up. And I'm going to ask you -- it needs to be turned to the right, a quarter turn to the right. That's it. Can you blow it up? Okay, that's good.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Professor Wright, do you recognise this site?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. This is the surface -- the buried surface on which these 15 or so individuals lay at Kozluk. Behind the bodies, you can see the bank which is not excavated. That's the extension of the soil that covered these bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. There's a -- we have this way of marking on the screen here. You should get some help. There's a little pen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The court usher will assist you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as best you can, and I know it's a two-dimensional --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you continue and make the markings, please have a seat. And Mr. Tolimir, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. The professor had already started answering, but I had raised my hand. I would like to ask the Prosecutor to state the grounds for this re-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, can you give us and Mr. Tolimir any reference?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Page 32, line 14 to 25, it had to do with bodies at Kozluk, and this is particularly to the question asked by Judge Nyambe that I -- this is the photograph that I had offered to help explain some of what Professor Wright was explaining when he talked about things, which I'll get in for him to answer and not myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think that is sufficient. You should proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you -- as best you can, can you draw with a line where the actual level of the ground was that you took away from these bodies when you uncovered them? It should leave a line on the screen.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There we go.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: That sort of line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. We see that red horizontal line. So underneath that red line, there would have been what?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: There would have been soil which had been put over the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us, how is it that you're able to take soil off bodies like that and leave this scene with -- that looks so undisturbed? How can you do that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: We're archaeologists. I mean, we know how to remove soil from objects.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And can you -- do you see any markings that you have concluded were made by heavy equipment?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Well, not in -- not in the area of the bodies, but you can see -- can I mark this edge here [marks]? This is an edge of a deep trench which cut through the bodies, so I think it's this individual who was complete except for one leg that must have been taken away when this trench was put in before -- was put in and removed other bodies. It cut across this one individual. This area which shows the main line of bodies was totally undisturbed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we understand that you have taken the soil off what we can see in some instances are skeletons. This dark trench thing that you've outlined, who made that trench?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Well, it was made before we ever got to the site and was filled in again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so how did you create that, as archaeologists? Can you just explain that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: We -- we can tell where a cut -- a trench cut has occurred, and we remove the soil out of that until we get to the bottom. And on the bottom, we found, in fact, the marks -- the buckets of heavy machinery. So I interpret this is the trench which was used to remove bodies, of which it left just this little extension showing the surface on which bodies are now lying. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, for the sake of the record, it would be helpful if you can ask the witness to identify the different lines with an A, B, C, or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you just do that and tell us which ones you're identifying, so the record is clear?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I'm not sure, Your Honour, how I do this. For instance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just put --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'll draw a line around the deep trench and call that A [marks], which cut through the bodies which lie on the surface, which I'll call B [marks], and were then covered up by this soil, which I'll call C [marks]. Is that adequate?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And perhaps the letter D where you supposed that there was a leg taken away.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I'll put D [marks], yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was this individual here. In my report, I do include a map of that distribution of bodies, and so it's possible to see, from that, which of these individuals was damaged. But I can't -- without going through my report, I can't add any more at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I don't think we need to do that at the moment. And so I would offer this photograph into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received with the markings.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1015.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And just to further clarify: You've testified about what -- I'm not sure -- what grave is this again, just --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: This is Kozluk --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: -- which we did in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: From your view of what we're looking at right here, did you make any determination whether any of these individuals were shot where they are now, in-situ?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: We could see some injury that I, you know, inexpert, in a non-expert way, would attribute to gun-shot wounds. The morgue would have determined that finally. But what we did notice, with metal detectors, were that there were bullets embedded in the soil underneath these bodies down to a depth of about 10 centimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we can just put this one into evidence and have another blank of this up there for just one more use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you do that, Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Can you just clarify for me how -- it's gone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we get the markings back?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: I can try without the markings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Oh, it will be possible to have the markings back. P1015.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Okay, let me try without the markings. Can you explain how that trench, or ditch, came about, firstly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was dug by heavy machinery, and there are tooth marks in the bottom. It was done -- it was done before the site was covered over. We saw nothing on the surface except soil that filled up this trench and which covered the bodies. Now, I know, from aerial imagery that I have seen, that this work was done sometime in -- this trench was almost certainly part of the work that was done at the site in October 1995, which would have taken the bodies -- the rest of the bodies away to sites like Cancari Road 3 that had all that broken glass. So what I'm looking at is a trench which is consistent with the removal of the bodies, but I don't have a direct way of dating when that particular trench was put in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Where would this soil to cover the grave have come from? Did it collect naturally or it was put over the bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I'm sure that it was put over the bodies, because none of the bodies showed damage by scavenging animals. The soil that was put over the bodies is a mixture of the -- well, perhaps I could just start again. The whole site is in a sand quarry. There are hollows occurring naturally, and the people from the town would collect sand and silt, but also there was building rubble which covered these bodies that could not have come locally. So some material, including clay and building rubble, must have been brought from a settlement to help cover the bodies. But in general, there's material suitable for covering the bodies all over the place and would just have to be bulldozed over them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We can leave this photo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you remember or can you tell from this photo whether any of the victims in this photo had ligatures, had their hands tied behind their back?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I'm relying on my memory. Yes, but the official records would have to be consulted. I think my diagram -- if I can consult my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: In my report on Kozluk, which is, I think -- I don't know how you assign the evidence number to say what I'm referring to, but it's got on the front stamped "00912156."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just a moment. We'll get a number. P871, for the record.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I say in my report we -- the particular exposure that we're looking at in that picture is re-labelled "KK2," and I say some executed bodies lay undisturbed on a surface that was subsequently covered with soil. The limbs -- the reasons for concluding that the bodies were executed on that spot and not dumped there are that limbs are not disarranged, but I don't comment, so far as I can see, on whether these individuals had ligatures or blindfolds, but that would be contained within the logs. I mean, those individuals could be identified. My memory is that some of them had their hands tied behind their back, but I could not be confident in that recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Any memory about blindfolds in this site?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: In general at Kozluk, many individuals were blindfolded. And this is merely an extension of the main Kozluk site. I've got the numbers, again, in my report of the number of bodies that we saw which were blindfolded and had ligatures, and I think it was something like 42 per cent had ligatures and 20 per cent had blindfolds. That's my approximate -- my memory of the approximate number. Some had both.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Could we just blow this up a couple of times just slowly so we can get a little closer look at this grave?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you indicate on which part?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think if we can use the -- the upper half is good. One more shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you just describe what we're seeing there. It's hard, I know, looking at this mass.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: We're seeing complete bodies, most of them lying on their back on a surface which contains, embedded below the bodies, bullets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Professor, I thank you very much. I have no further question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Professor, the Chamber is grateful for your attendance here and that you have helped us with your expertise. You are now free to return to your normal activities, and our thanks again for your attendance. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, is there another witness available for today?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. We -- we've been trying to recover from -- and it's nice to finish a witness a little earlier than normal. We're still recovering from the longer witnesses and the people we've cancelled as a result. But we do think we can fill a good part of tomorrow and the next day with some important video that we've been planning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, the witness may -- yes. Thank you very much. Sorry, we just continued with our procedural matters. Goodbye.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We have some important video that we have been planning on showing, that we've been discussing this with Mr. Gajic, and as well as an exhibit of stills taken from those videos that we think will be very helpful for the Trial Chamber to help analyse and review those videos. And so we have two investigators that we would start tomorrow with. I think first will be Dusan Janc. And you recall he's in the middle of cross-examination on another topic, but I think we've -- in discussions with Mr. Gajic, that we -- that further cross-examination on that topic can still be, you know, put off for a while. They've got lots of material that we've given to them that I think they're still digesting. So we do have the videos, brief explanations of those videos, authentications of those videos, as we have seen that the Court would like from some of your comments on other documents, so that's our plan for the next two days. But, unfortunately, we don't have anything right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I must confess we are not complaining that we are finishing a little bit earlier today. But did I understand you correctly, that tomorrow we will continue with the cross-examination of Mr. Janc, or are you requesting to go back to examination-in-chief first?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm sorry. We're -- we're going to the examination-in-chief on Mr. Janc on the playing of these videos. It was our understanding that you would appreciate a little background on where these videos came from, a bit about what they are, so that they make more sense when you see them, so it was our intention to have Mr. Janc to provide that bit of background and authentication prior to the playing of the videos. And we're not suggesting his continued cross-examination. We have not yet reached an agreement on when that would be appropriate, with the Defence. But we continue to talk about that, and we have lots more witnesses to take up time before we get to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir or Mr. Gajic, are you in agreement with this proposal by Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we are. We do not know what is to be presented. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Then I take it that this will be part -- another part of the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We have to adjourn for today, and we will resume tomorrow at quarter past 2.00 in this courtroom. We adjourn.
